The first time I noticed time behaving oddly, it wasn’t dramatic. No clocks shattered, no sky split open, no sudden chorus of angels or alarms. It was smaller than that—more insulting, really. I was standing in a grocery store aisle, staring at a shelf of cereal I didn’t need, when I realized I’d been staring for what felt like several minutes, yet the person behind me had only shifted their weight once, as if the universe had a metronome and I’d briefly slipped out of alignment with it.

I’ve learned, over the years, that strange experiences rarely arrive with a siren. They arrive with the quiet confidence of something ordinary—until you try to define it. Until you ask, “What just happened?” and discover the question itself is suddenly hard to hold.

That’s the thing: we think the world is made of objects. But maybe it’s made of relationships—between your attention and your perception, between your body and gravity, between what you expect and what you get. When something nudges one relationship, the others react. A moment of confusion can turn into a lingering suspicion that reality is a little more negotiable than we pretend.

After that day, I began to treat everyday life like a set of clues. I didn’t become paranoid or frantic. If anything, I became patient. I started paying attention to tiny mismatches: the slightly delayed echo in a hallway; the way certain songs seemed to anticipate my thoughts; the feeling—sometimes strong, sometimes faint—that I was arriving at a memory before I remembered it.

I told myself this was just how brains work. Brains are prediction machines. They fill in blanks. They smooth over inconsistencies. They make meaning out of randomness. So perhaps the odd time-stretching I’d felt was the mind’s way of compensating for stress, boredom, caffeine, or whatever invisible chemical weather had drifted through that aisle.

But then came the second incident, and it didn’t fit any of my tidy explanations.

It was late—later than I meant it to be, the way all the nights that matter usually are. I had been working on something unimportant, which is to say I’d been working on something that didn’t require courage. The kind of work where mistakes can be fixed later. I remember the light on my desk. It was the color of late afternoon even though the window had gone fully dark. I remember the sound of the fridge cycling on and off, like a patient animal breathing in sleep.

And then I remember a sensation, almost physical: a tug behind my eyes, as if someone had pulled a thread in my skull and the fabric of the moment had shifted.

When it settled, my screen looked different. Not dramatically. Not in a way you could point to and say, “Aha—time travel!” It was just that I had a note open that I didn’t remember writing. A sentence at the top, in my handwriting—because I recognize my handwriting the way you recognize your own name—finished a thought I hadn’t begun.

I stared at it until it stopped being a message and started being an accusation.

The sentence said: *You’ll forget the feeling if you don’t record it now.*

There are two kinds of fear. The fear that something will happen, and the fear that something already happened and you missed it. This was the second kind. I didn’t know what I was supposed to do with the knowledge, so I did what I always do when overwhelmed: I tried to solve it like a puzzle.

I searched for evidence. I checked timestamps, version history, anything that could account for the note’s existence. I checked my email, my documents, cloud storage logs. Nothing obvious. The note had the right metadata for being there. It wasn’t a glitch in my software. It wasn’t some prank. It wasn’t even a near miss—there was no half-baked entry or corrupt data. It was clean, deliberate, and oddly concerned.

If I had woken up to the note in the morning, I might have dismissed it as an old reminder, an artifact from a previous attempt to organize my brain. But the note arrived during the moment I was experiencing, which meant either my perception was failing—again—or something else was reaching across a boundary.

That was the first time I considered the possibility that “time” isn’t a line we travel along. Maybe it’s a space we move through, and sometimes the movement intersects with other versions of ourselves—other runs of the same day, other outcomes.

You can make all the jokes you want about paradoxes, but the discomfort remains: if you believe your mind is capable of reaching backward or forward, even slightly, then you have to admit that certainty is a luxury. It isn’t yours by default. It’s something you earn by how carefully you look, how honestly you measure, how willing you are to abandon your favorite explanations when they stop matching the evidence.

In the weeks that followed, I began to collect not just memories but sensations. I kept a notebook—not because I wanted to become a mystic, but because I wanted to control for myself. I wrote down the days when my attention lagged behind events. I wrote down the days when it seemed to leap ahead. I wrote down what I was doing, what I ate, what I felt in my body—tight throat, heavy shoulders, a sudden warmth in my palms.

I expected patterns. Brains love patterns. They also love stories that soothe them. But the patterns were slippery. Sometimes the “feeling of tugging” occurred after sleep deprivation. Sometimes after a pleasant conversation. Sometimes after nothing at all that seemed important.

The only consistent element was the note’s tone—the careful urgency, like someone trying to keep you from forgetting something important.

I started to suspect that whatever was happening wasn’t trying to impress me. It wasn’t trying to change my life with spectacle. It was doing something more intimate and more frightening: it was trying to communicate.

Not in words, necessarily. Often it was only in the direction of thought. I would be standing in the kitchen, deciding whether to take an apple or a banana, and suddenly I would feel a brief certainty that if I chose wrong, I would regret it later—not because the fruit matters, but because the decision would alter the chain of attention. I would do something minor, and later realize I had done it in a different mood than I intended, as if I’d been guided into a mental posture I would need.

It’s hard to explain this without sounding like I’m claiming supernatural powers. I don’t believe I’m special. If anything, the experience made me feel smaller. It suggested that the world doesn’t care about my narratives, only about the mechanics beneath them.

Maybe that’s why the strangest part wasn’t the time weirdness. It was the ethical implication.

If the future—or another version of it—can reach me, then my choices aren’t just mine. Or rather, they are mine and not mine at the same time. The person writing the note, if it was me, was me with knowledge I didn’t yet possess. That knowledge could be good—could help me avoid harm—or it could be irrelevant, the way a weather forecast is irrelevant if you don’t change your plans.

Either way, the question becomes: what do you do with guidance you didn’t ask for?

One night, after months of collecting clues and trying not to become the kind of person who talks about “timelines” like they’re brands, I finally chose to test something. I sat at my desk and wrote, in the notebook, a sentence I hoped I wouldn’t forget. Then I wrote another sentence beneath it, a kind of invitation to whatever mechanism was listening.

I wrote: *If you can reach me, show up in a way that doesn’t scare me. Show me something small and kind.*

I didn’t expect results. I expected confirmation bias—my brain taking my wish and turning it into a pattern. I expected nothing and was ready to dismiss everything.

But on the third day after that, I received a message from a friend I hadn’t spoken to in a year. The message wasn’t elaborate. It was simple: *Hey. I keep thinking about you. Are you okay?*

We talked for an hour. It turns out they’d been going through something and had almost decided not to reach out because the timing felt awkward and the world is full of reasons to delay. They said they’d felt, briefly, like they needed to send the message before a certain deadline—like a small tug behind their eyes.

They used different words, and they didn’t know anything about my notebook or my weird time feelings. But the overlap in tone—the same urgency, the same softness—hit me harder than any explanation ever could.

It made me believe, briefly and responsibly, that the message wasn’t about changing the universe’s rules. It was about keeping people connected. About reminding us that attention can be a form of love. About showing that the strangest phenomena we experience often point back to the simplest human need: to be seen, and to see each other in return.

Maybe time is negotiable. Maybe consciousness is stranger than we admit. Or maybe I’m just learning how to pay attention, slowly, honestly, until my mind stops dismissing patterns and starts noticing the ways we already reach across distances we can’t measure.

Either way, I’ve kept the notebook. Not as proof of magic, but as a small ritual of humility. Whenever the tugging sensation returns—behind my eyes, in the space between expectation and reality—I write down what I feel. I write it down even if it makes no sense yet. I write it down because forgetting is the easiest thing in the world, and remembering might be the bravest.

And every once in a while, when a coincidence becomes too aligned to ignore, I allow myself the gentlest thought: that perhaps the future isn’t only something we wait for.

Perhaps it’s something we practice.

Perhaps it’s already here, in the way we choose what to pay attention to, in the way we decide whether to reach out, and in the way we keep showing up—again and again—trying to be the kind of person who doesn’t need to be warned twice.
